Measuring Brand in B2B

The Commercial SystemPart 13

By lowob · 25 August 2026 · 9-minute read · Growth

Measuring brand in B2B means tracking whether buyers think of you, and rank you, before they contact anyone. That ranking now happens early: 6sense's 2025 survey of more than 4,000 buyers found 94% of buying groups had ranked preferred vendors before first contact, and the favourite usually won. Attribution systems see only what happens after that moment, which is why brand budgets are cut first and defended worst. Five measures hold up in B2B: share of search, shortlist rate, mental availability against buying situations, branded demand, and win rate and price when the buyer already knew you. Each needs adapting when a market has a few hundred buyers rather than millions.

Performance spend comes with a dashboard. Brand spend comes with a belief, and when the quarter is tight, the belief loses. This piece is not an argument for spending more on brand; our explainer Brand vs performance marketing covers how the two work on different timescales. The question here is what a 50- to 500-person B2B firm can measure, cheaply and honestly, to know whether its brand is doing its job.

Why brand goes unmeasured in B2B

Three structural reasons keep brand off the dashboard.

Attribution only sees the in-market few. The B2B Institute, LinkedIn's research unit, worked with John Dawes of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute on what they call the 95:5 rule. Their illustration: if most companies switch business banks about once every five years, roughly 20% are in market in a year, about 2% in a month and about 1% in a fortnight. Dawes's own May 2021 report puts the quarterly figure at something like 5%, reasoning from corporations changing providers such as their principal bank or law firm around once every five years. Attribution tools record the clicks and form fills of that small in-market group. The memory built among everyone else does not appear until months later, and then it appears as "direct" or "organic".

Spending skews to activation. Les Binet and Peter Field's analysis of B2B cases in the IPA Databank, published by the B2B Institute, found B2B businesses grew best with about 46% of budget on brand building and 54% on activation, and noted that spending tends to drift toward activation because sales targets are more pressing. Our earlier piece suggests a smaller firm still finding its first channel may start nearer 75:25. Either way, the drift is real and it happens by default.

The sample is small. A consumer brand can run a tracker on thousands of respondents. A firm selling to 400 mid-market manufacturers cannot. Most B2B brand measurement fails not because the measures are wrong but because they were borrowed from consumer markets without adjustment.

What the evidence says brand decides

The case for measuring brand rests on where B2B decisions are now made.

FindingSourceWhat it implies
94% of buying groups ranked preferred vendors before first contact6sense, 2025 Buyer Experience Report, 4,000+ buyersThe shortlist is set before sales can influence it
The preferred vendor chosen before seller contact wins about 80% of deals; buyers bought from the favourite 77% of the time6sense, 2025Being the favourite matters more than being on the list
67% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience; 45% used AI in a recent purchaseGartner, March 2026, 646 buyersMore of the early research happens where you cannot see it
Brands whose share of voice exceeds their share of market tend to growBinet and Field, IPA Databank B2B casesBrand spend relative to competitors is a growth input
Campaigns aimed at fame and mental availability outperform othersBinet and FieldBrand objectives should be measured as mental, not only behavioural

The 6sense and Gartner figures are self-reported surveys, so read them as direction rather than precision. The direction is consistent: a buyer forms a preference from memory, peers, reviews and AI assistants, and arrives at the first sales conversation with a ranking. Brand decides your place in it.

If the shortlist is set before first contact, the first measure of brand is whether you were on it.

Five measures that hold up

No single brand number is enough. The five below work together, and each answers a different question.

MeasureQuestion it answersData sourceCadenceMain failure mode
Share of searchIs interest in us rising relative to rivals?Search volume for your brand name against named competitorsMonthly, read quarterlyBreaks when volumes are tiny or the name is a common word
Shortlist rateWere we on the list before first contact?A required field at first meeting: "who else are you considering, and had you heard of us?"MonthlySellers skip the field unless it is short and reviewed
Mental availabilityDo buyers think of us in the situations that trigger a purchase?Survey of category buyers against a list of buying situationsTwice a yearToo few respondents, or situations written in your language rather than the buyer's
Branded demandAre buyers seeking us by name?Branded search clicks, direct inbound, "heard of us from" answersMonthlyPaid branded search inflating the number
Known-buyer win rate and priceDoes familiarity pay at close?Win rate and discount for deals where the buyer knew you first, against those where they did notQuarterlyToo few deals per quarter to separate noise

Share of search. Les Binet presented this at the IPA's EffWorks Global in October 2020. Across automotive, energy and mobile handsets, a brand's share of category search tracked its market share, rises tended to precede share gains, and the lead could be as long as a year in cars. Binet called it "by no means a silver bullet": price and other factors affect conversion. In B2B it works best in categories with real search volume, such as software, payments or logistics, and poorly in niches where monthly searches are in the dozens.

Shortlist rate. This is the cheapest measure most firms are not collecting. Add two fields to the first-meeting record in the CRM: which competitors the buyer is considering, and whether they knew of you before outreach. Over a year, the share of first meetings where you were already known and already shortlisted is a brand measure your sales team generates for free. It also improves the closed-lost record, which our explainer What is a closed-lost reason? covers.

Mental availability against buying situations. Jenni Romaniuk's work with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, adapted for B2B by the B2B Institute, frames brand as a network of category entry points: the situations in which a buyer starts to need the category. A logistics platform's entry points might be "a carrier fails peak season" or "we are expanding into a new country". The method is to list the situations, prune those with low credibility, high competition or low frequency, and survey buyers on which brands come to mind for each. The measure is how many situations you are linked to, and by how many buyers.

Branded demand. Report paid branded search separately, or the brand team is measuring its own media budget.

Known-buyer win rate and price. The commercial test of brand is whether familiarity changes the close. If buyers who knew you before first contact win more often, or need less discount, the brand is earning money a finance team can see. Our piece Attribution vs incrementality explains why this comparison is suggestive rather than causal.

Measuring brand when the market is small

The Ehrenberg-Bass Institute's November 2025 report Easy to Find surveyed more than 500 B2B marketers in the US and UK and found they used an average of 3.7 sales channels, and that about 30% could not estimate how much of their revenue came from their core product. If a firm cannot see its own portfolio, it is unlikely to see its brand clearly. The fix is to scale the measures to the market.

Market shapeExampleMeasures that workMeasures to skip
Thousands of buyers, real search volumeMid-market software, paymentsAll five; share of search as the lead indicatorNone
Hundreds of named accountsIndustrial components, specialist dataShortlist rate, known-buyer win rate, a short survey of named accountsShare of search; large trackers
Dozens of buyersInfrastructure, enterprise platformsShortlist rate, structured win-loss interviews, analyst and partner mentionsAny survey-based tracker
New category, little searchEmerging technology, early AI toolingMental availability for the problem, not the category; branded demand from zeroShare of search until volume exists

For a market of a few hundred accounts, a survey of 80 to 150 buyers twice a year can be enough to see movement in mental availability, provided the same situations are tested each time. For a market of dozens, the honest answer is that brand is measured one account at a time, through win-loss interviews and what partners and analysts say about you. Our explainer What is win-loss analysis? covers the interview method.

With 45% of buyers using AI in a recent purchase, how assistants describe you is now part of your brand; How LLMs choose sources covers how to check.

Brand spend as a recorded decision

Brand budgets are lost because they are defended once a year, from memory, against a dashboard. The alternative is to treat brand spend the way The Build Order treats any commercial decision: written down with a reason, an owner, an expected outcome and a date to check it (The commercial decisions worth recording).

A brand decision record has five fields:

FieldExample entry
DecisionHold brand spend at 35% of programme budget for four quarters
ReasonShortlist rate fell from roughly half to roughly a third of first meetings over the past year
OwnerHead of marketing; reviewed with the revenue leader
Expected outcomeShortlist rate recovers; share of search stops falling against the two nearest rivals
Check dateQuarterly, with a full review at four quarters

The argument with finance is no longer "brand matters" but "we expected these two numbers to move by this date; here is what happened". If they did not move, the record shows that too. Stop reporting reach covers why impressions belong outside this record.

The quarterly commercial review in Part 6 of this series is the natural home for the check. The KPI set in Part 7 should carry at least one brand measure, usually shortlist rate, so that it sits beside pipeline rather than in a separate marketing report.

Illustrative example: a software firm finds its brand problem in the CRM
Decision
Add two required fields to the first-meeting record (competitors considered; known before outreach) and report shortlist rate monthly.
Reason and owner
Paid search costs were rising and win rates falling, with no brand measure to explain either. Owned by the head of revenue operations.
What changed
After two quarters the firm saw it was known before outreach in under a third of first meetings, and that those deals closed with less discount. Brand spend was moved into the quarterly review with an expected shortlist rate and a check date.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B software firm, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Measure the moment before first contact. Most buyers have ranked vendors by then; shortlist rate tells you where you stood.
  • Use several measures, scaled to the market. Share of search needs volume; small markets need named-account surveys and win-loss interviews.
  • Separate paid from earned branded demand. Otherwise the brand number is a media budget in disguise.
  • Record brand spend as a decision. An expected outcome and a check date turn an annual argument into a quarterly review.
Gateway card

Before your next brand budget review

  • Shortlist and "known before outreach" fields added to the first-meeting record
  • Share of search tracked against two or three named rivals, if volume allows
  • Five to ten buying situations listed in the buyer's language
  • Win rate and discount compared for known and unknown buyers
  • Brand spend recorded with an expected outcome and a check date

Common questions

How do you measure brand awareness in B2B?

Combine share of search, a shortlist field captured at first sales contact, a survey of category buyers against buying situations, branded demand reported separately from paid search, and win rate for buyers who knew you before outreach.

What is share of search?

Your brand's share of search volume among named competitors in a category. Les Binet's 2020 IPA work found it tracked market share in three categories and often moved first, though it needs meaningful search volume to work.

What is the 95:5 rule in B2B marketing?

A rule of thumb from the B2B Institute and the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute that only a small share of business buyers are in market at any time, so most marketing should build memory among the larger group who will buy later.

How much should a B2B company spend on brand versus performance?

Binet and Field's B2B analysis points to about 46% brand and 54% activation for established firms. Smaller firms still finding a channel often start with more performance spend and shift toward brand as the channel proves itself.

Sources and notes

  • 6sense, 2025 Buyer Experience Report, via Business Wire, 12 November 2025. Vendor research; survey of 4,000+ buyers; self-reported.
  • Gartner, sales survey on rep-free buying, 9 March 2026. Analyst survey of 646 B2B buyers, fieldwork August to September 2025.
  • Marketing Week, Weinberg and Lombardo, The 95:5 rule is the new 60:40 rule. Authors lead research at the LinkedIn-funded B2B Institute; the purchase-cycle figures are illustrative.
  • LinkedIn B2B Institute, Binet and Field, The 5 Principles of Growth in B2B Marketing. Based on IPA Databank B2B cases 1998 to 2018; sample skews to UK and larger budgets.
  • Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, Advertising effectiveness and the 95-5 rule: most B2B buyers are not in the market right now, John Dawes, May 2021. The original report behind the 95:5 rule, produced for LinkedIn's B2B Institute; the in-market share is an estimate from replacement cycles.
  • LinkedIn, How B2B marketing really drives growth, 16 October 2019. Platform summary of the Binet and Field study; source of the 46:54 split; LinkedIn sells B2B advertising.
  • IPA, Binet presents fast, cheap, predictive Share of Search metric, 14 October 2020. Three consumer categories; B2B application is by extension.
  • LinkedIn B2B Institute, Category Entry Points in B2B. Written with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute; method guide rather than a study.
  • Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, Easy to Find: Being Where B2B Buying Happens, November 2025. Survey of 500+ B2B marketers in the US and UK.
  • The market-shape table and survey sizes are lowob's guidance, not findings from these sources.
